catalog_quote: En resumen, la lengua amahuaca presenta un rasgo de tono alto que contrasta con la ausencia de tono. No hay tonos bajos ni medios en la lengua. Este rasgo es de carácter léxico, en el sentido de que no es posible predecir la posición del tono en una palabra morfológicamente simple. La TBU del amahuaca es la sílaba. [p. 99] ... En amahuaca, la evidencia apunta a que los pies son formados de izquierda a derecha. [p. 101] ... podemos decir, hasta el momento, no contamos con evidencia que nos permita postular un acento primario para la palabra amahuaca, lo que problematizaría postular un rasgo de acento prototípico para la lengua en cuestión ... Por lo tanto, cautamente, en este artículo hablamos de estructura métrica y no de acento en amahuaca. [p. 102] ... la estructura métrica descrita para la palabra amahuaca no satisface —hasta donde hemos podido determinar— el principio de culminatividad, que supone la posibilidad de identificar una sílaba de máxima prominencia prosódica (acento primario) en las palabras con dos o más pies métricos bien formados. ... Por ello, en este artículo no nos referimos a la estructura métrica de la palabra amahuaca como “acento” (stress). [p. 105]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: En resumen, la lengua amahuaca presenta un rasgo de tono alto que contrasta con la ausencia de tono. No hay tonos bajos ni medios en la lengua. Este rasgo es de carácter léxico, en el sentido de que no es posible predecir la posición del tono en una palabra morfológicamente simple. La TBU del amahuaca es la sílaba. [p. 99] [...] En amahuaca, la evidencia apunta a que los pies son formados de izquierda a derecha. [p. 101] [...] hasta el momento, no contamos con evidencia que nos permita postular un acento primario para la palabra amahuaca [...] Por lo tanto, cautamente, en este artículo hablamos de estructura métrica y no de acento en amahuaca. [p. 102]
new_statements.translation: In sum, Amahuaca has a high-tone feature that contrasts with the absence of tone. There are no low or mid tones in the language. This feature is lexical, in the sense that the position of the tone in a morphologically simple word cannot be predicted. The TBU of Amahuaca is the syllable. [...] In Amahuaca the evidence points to feet being built from left to right. [...] so far we have no evidence that would let us posit a primary stress for the Amahuaca word [...] Therefore, cautiously, in this article we speak of metrical structure and not of stress in Amahuaca.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Amahuaca is a one-tone (H vs. Ø) language: every word carries at least one H, no two adjacent H, and in simple roots the H sits on a lexically fixed, unpredictable syllable (11 patterns over 6 syllable shapes; bisyllables with closed final syllable and (C)ViʔVi words never have final H). Independently, the word is parsed into trochaic feet from left to right (odd syllables = strong: they keep nasal codas and resist weakening; even syllables = weak). In morphologically complex words the lexical H is moved off even syllables onto foot heads. The authors find no syllable of maximal prominence (no primary stress) and therefore decline to call the metrical structure 'stress'. Older analysis (Russell & Russell 1959: 128): stress is non-phonemic and falls on the high-toned syllable, or on the first of two consecutive high-toned syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; every odd-numbered syllable is a trochaic foot head with equal prominence (degenerate one-syllable feet allowed), and no head is singled out as primary (pp. 101-102, 104-105).
new_statements.exceptions: Interjections such as hɨnʔɨn 'yes' carry a final H where closed-final bisyllables otherwise never do (fn. 6, p. 96); monosyllabic V words are realised as extra-long V́V to satisfy the one-H-per-word requirement (p. 96); some variation in nasal-coda behaviour (p. 100); H-vs-Ø difference in HØ words is subtle, less marked in men's speech (fn. 7, p. 99).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, elicited citation forms (nouns for lexical tone; roots plus monosyllabic bound morphemes/enclitics for metrical tone), 1030 recorded tokens from 5 adult speakers, 2017-2023, Ucayali (Pucallpa workshop); phrase-level tone sandhi (Russell & Russell 1959) and clitic irregularities deferred to work in prep.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Peruvian Amahuaca (Ucayali: Sepahua, Inuya, Yurúa; earlier SIL work at Yarinacocha), glottocode amah1246; Sparing-Chávez 2012: 2 (as reported by Zariquiey et al. 2024: 80) claims no significant dialect variation, which Zariquiey et al. doubt. The 2024 article's speakers were recorded in Pucallpa/Ucayali; Clem 2019's in Sepahua (origins Sepahua, Inuya, Yuruá). No separate dialect glottocode involved.

new_statements.quote: Un elemento fonológico que no ha sido tratado casi en su totalidad es el que tiene que ver con el tono. El amahuaca registra un sistema tonal de dos niveles fonémicos y muestra un sandhi bien elaborado, el cual depende de la clase sintáctica a la que pertenecen las palabras que ocurren en secuencia dentro de la oración. [p. 11] | El tono alto se representa por (´) sobre la vocal. [p. 65] | Las reglas que rigen el tono sandhi no se presentan en esta tesis, pero pueden ser vistas en "Syntactotonemics in amahuaca", (Robert and Delores Russell, (1959)). [p. 66]
new_statements.translation: A phonological element that has been left almost entirely untreated is tone. Amahuaca has a tonal system of two phonemic levels and shows a well-elaborated sandhi, which depends on the syntactic class of the words occurring in sequence within the sentence. [p. 11] | High tone is represented by (´) over the vowel. [p. 65] | The rules governing tone sandhi are not presented in this thesis but can be seen in 'Syntactotonemics in Amahuaca' (Robert and Delores Russell 1959). [p. 66]
new_statements.citation: Russell, Robert L. (1965). A Transformational Grammar of Amahuaca (Pano). Columbus University. Ohio State University. iii+112 pp.
new_statements.locator: Introducción p. 11 (p. 11; the scanned text); Cap. II morfofonémica p. 65 (acute = high tone) and p. 66 (sandhi deferred); Notas p. 98 n. 1 and p. 99 Cap. II n. 1 (tone marks omitted in most examples); file

new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the catalog's tonal coding (two phonemic tone levels, tone sandhi) and is silent on stress/metrical structure, so it neither supports nor contradicts Zariquiey et al. 2024's left-to-right trochaic footing; the odd/even-syllable conditioning of allophony (pp. 65-66) is the same parity sensitivity Hyde 1980 and Zariquiey et al. describe, but Russell does not call it stress. Reading taken from the unrevised Spanish translation; the English original was not seen.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar treats Amahuaca as a two-level tone language with syntactically conditioned tone sandhi and explicitly sets tone aside; it says nothing about word stress or accent placement (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent acent|prosod|intensid|stress = 0 hits; the only 'énfasis' is the clause constituent INDICADOR DE ENFASIS, p. 25). The tentative phonetic rules Ft1-Ft4 (pp. 65-66) are conditioned on whether a syllable is odd- or even-numbered in the word, i.e. on syllable-count parity, not on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none (tone not treated; reader referred to Russell & Russell 1959 and Osborn 1948)
new_statements.identity_note: Russell's data: Amahuaca of Varadero, headwaters of the Inuya river (Loreto/Ucayali, Peru), collected 1953-1964 under SIL; same Peruvian Amahuaca [amc] as the catalog sources (Zariquiey et al. work with present-day speakers; Hyde 1980 SIL Peru).

new_statements.translation: In this vocabulary I have used the written accent to indicate high tone, as an aid to the Spanish speaker in pronouncing Amahuaca. For more information see the article on tone in Amahuaca by Richard Hyde and Eugene Loos. | -ma negative (applies to roots with an even number of syllables) ... -mama negative (applies to roots with an odd number of syllables). | -yan/-yantax are used with roots that have an odd number of syllables and -yana with the rest.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the existing statement (Zariquiey, Valenzuela & Angulo 2024: a single high tone contrasting with absence of tone, lexically placed, plus metrical structure): Hyde marks only a high tone with the acute and treats it as lexical (written per entry); the syllable-parity allomorphy is compatible with the binary footing Zariquiey et al. describe. Silent on stress placement itself; the catalog record's rule field is empty, so nothing is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The acute accent in the dictionary marks lexical high tone, not stress; no statement on where stress falls. The grammatical appendix records suffix allomorphy conditioned by the parity of the root's syllable count (even vs odd) and by mono- vs polysyllabic roots (-canh / -cánhan), i.e. binary metrical grouping, but never names stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works concern Peruvian Amahuaca as worked on by SIL (Russell, Hyde, Loos; Yarinacocha/Ucayali-Purús headwaters communities); no distinct dialect is singled out. Hyde 1980 was read in its 2008 second edition (archive.org scan), whose text reproduces the 1980 preliminary edition.

sources.note: Whole article is on word prosody (1030 tokens, 5 speakers, Praat): one lexical tone H vs Ø whose position in simple words is unpredictable (p. 99, Table 3 pp. 97-98); trochaic feet built left-to-right, diagnosed by nasal-coda loss in even syllables (pp. 100-101, (17)); no evidence for a primary stress, culminativity unmet, so authors speak of 'estructura métrica' not 'acento' (p. 102, pp. 104-105); H shifts off even (weak) syllables in complex words (pp. 102-104).

sources.note: p. 128: 'Amahuaca has a register system with two tonemes.. Phonetic stress placement is dependent upon phonemic tone. In general, a syllable with high tone, or the first of two consecutive syllables with high tone receives predominant stress.' Fn. 1 (p. 158) says stress is non-phonemic in their analysis B (phonemic in Osborn's A); fn. 3 refers fuller stress rules to their unpublished ms 'Allophonic Variation in Amahuaca (Pano) with a Brief Vocabulary'; fn. 5: syllable is the unit of tone placement. Scan from Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú, existing scanned layer.

sources.note: Silent on stress placement. On tone it is compatible with the existing statement (Zariquiey et al. 2024: lexical high tone contrasting with its absence) though it phrases the system as two tone levels rather than privative H. It points to Russell & Russell 1959 (already held by the project here; p. 128 there: stress placement depends on phonemic tone, the high-toned syllable or the first of two consecutive high-toned syllables gets predominant stress) as the place where tone and prominence are treated.
